Zadie Smith. Born in 1975, a British-Jamaican novelist and essayist known for her energetic, formally playful, and multiethnic narratives that blend postmodern technique with accessible storytelling. Her debut, White Teeth, published in 2000, announced her as a major voice in contemporary fiction, combining postcolonial themes, multicultural London, humor, and formal innovation. Her essays on reading, writing, and technology are widely influential.

White Teeth traces three interwoven families—Jamaican, Bengali, Jewish—across decades in contemporary London. The novel celebrates difference while interrogating the myths of multiculturalism and belonging. Smith employs playful narrative framing, unreliable narration, and self-aware digressions. Her style is less austere than Pynchon or Wallace but shares their formal sophistication and thematic ambition. Swing Time, published in 2016, meditates on friendship, performance, race, and the labor of dance. It braids autobiography, biography, and cultural criticism, exploring identity formation across continents. Her essays, collected in Feel Free, address reading, literature, AI, and identity with erudition and accessibility. She writes about postmodernism and literary difficulty with a voice that resists academic jargon. Changing My Mind, an earlier essay collection, contains influential pieces on Middlemarch, close reading, and the ethics of literary interpretation. Smith emphasizes the pleasure of reading and the human stakes of storytelling. Her work resists purely formalist aesthetics in favor of ethical and emotional engagement. She shares with David Foster Wallace a synthesis of postmodern difficulty with emotional sincerity, both prizing readerly pleasure and formal innovation. Her work is rooted in postcolonial concerns like those of Salman Rushdie, with whom she shares a diasporic perspective on identity and belonging.
